idiom_name: protocol declaration (requirements plus protocol-extension default implementations)
implementation_notes: A protocol states the methods, properties and subscripts a conforming type must provide; protocols have no storage, so a contract-only declaration is the natural Swift form and - unlike an abstract class - it can be adopted by structs and enums as well as classes. What replaces the classic base class is conformance plus, where useful, a protocol extension supplying default implementations; any Protocol is the existential box used for runtime polymorphism, while generics and some Protocol keep the contract static. Optional requirements exist only for Objective-C interop (@objc optional, class-only conformance), so in pure Swift optionality is expressed by splitting the protocol or by providing a default implementation in an extension.
pitfalls: A requirement that also has a default implementation in an extension dispatches dynamically through any Shape but statically when the concrete type is known, so an implementation that exists only on the concrete type can be silently bypassed.
any Shape boxes value types and may allocate; prefer a generic constraint or some Shape where the concrete type can stay known.
Protocols with Self or associated-type requirements cannot be used as existentials without type erasure (an AnyShape wrapper), which is where a contract needs a second, erased form.
@objc optional requirements force class-only conformance and turn every member into an optional; they are an Objective-C compatibility feature, not a Swift design tool.
